opus-5.5.text:
Well, it's been fascinating to watch, because for a long time, really for the first decade or so of DeepMind, AI was something only a fairly small group of researchers took seriously. We'd talk about AGI and people would kind of smile politely, as if it were science fiction. And then over the last few years there's been this enormous shift. Partly that's down to things like AlphaGo, which was a sort of Sputnik moment, especially in Asia, and then of course the chatbots and large language models, which put AI directly into people's hands for the first time.

So now, in the circles I move in, whether that's scientists, policymakers, or business leaders, everyone is aware of it. Almost too aware, in some ways. There's a lot of hype, and I think in the short term AI is probably somewhat overhyped, with lots of money chasing things that aren't quite ready. But in the medium to long term, I still think it's underappreciated how transformative it's going to be. People haven't fully internalized what it means to have systems that could help us cure diseases, discover new materials, and understand the universe itself.

And what I find interesting is that the public conversation tends to swing between extremes. Either it's utopian or it's doom. What I try to encourage is a more nuanced, scientific view: take the risks very seriously, both misuse by bad actors and the technical challenges of keeping these systems controllable as they get more capable, while also being clear about the incredible benefits. We need governments, academia, and civil society engaging with this thoughtfully, ideally with international cooperation, because this is a technology that's going to affect everyone on the planet.

r001.rationale: The response says AI is now widely known in Hassabis’s circles and that chatbots put AI into people’s hands, but it does not say that much of the wider public has yet to encounter AI.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, it's interesting, because I think there's a real gap between how the people I work with day to day think about AI and how the general public does. Within the research community, and especially at DeepMind, we've been thinking about this for a long time, twenty years in my case, and so the idea that AI could be the most transformative technology in human history is kind of taken as given. We've been living with it.

But outside those circles, I think awareness has really only arrived in the last few years, mostly through the chatbots, because that's the first time people could actually touch it, talk to it, see it do something that felt intelligent. Before that, even things like AlphaGo, which were a huge moment for us, were somewhat abstract to most people. Go is a beautiful game but not many people in the West play it.

And I'd say the awareness is still quite uneven. A lot of the public conversation is either overly hyped, in the sense that people think these systems are already general intelligence, or it's dismissive, people saying it's just autocomplete. The truth is somewhere in the middle and more nuanced than either. The systems are genuinely remarkable, but they also have real gaps, in planning, in reasoning, in reliability, and we're honest about that internally.

What I actually care about most is that the public conversation gets to a level where people can engage sensibly with the real questions. Because the decisions about how this technology gets deployed, what we want it to do for us, what guardrails we want, those shouldn't just be made by a small group of people in a few labs. I think we need philosophers, social scientists, economists, ordinary citizens, everyone, thinking carefully about this. And for that you need an informed public, not a frightened one and not a complacent one. That's partly why I spend time doing conversations like this one.

r001.rationale: It contrasts the research community’s long-standing familiarity with AI—Hassabis says they have been thinking about it for twenty years—with public awareness arriving only in the last few years, largely through chatbots.

astra-6.text:
I think it depends enormously on which circles you’re in. If you work in AI, you’re surrounded by people thinking about it every day, and it’s easy to assume that everyone else has the same awareness. But knowing about AI and understanding what these systems can actually do are quite different things.

People can be very impressed by a particular demonstration and then assume the system has a much broader understanding than it does. Or they encounter a mistake and dismiss the whole thing. The reality is more interesting: these systems have remarkable capabilities, but also quite surprising limitations.

So I think we have a responsibility to explain both clearly—to convey why we’re excited, while being honest about what we don’t yet understand.

r001.rationale: The response says AI workers are surrounded by AI and may assume others share their awareness, but it does not clearly say that much of the wider public has yet to encounter AI.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it depends enormously on which circles you’re in. If you’re working in AI, or you’re in the technology world, it can feel as though everyone is talking about it and understands how significant it might be. But that’s quite a narrow slice of society. Outside those circles, there’s a much wider range of awareness, from people who are very excited to people who haven’t really thought about it much at all.

And awareness isn’t necessarily the same as understanding. You can have a lot of attention on a particular breakthrough without a clear sense of what the system can actually do, where its limitations are, or how it might affect your life. I think we have a responsibility as researchers to explain those things clearly, including the uncertainties, so that the wider public can participate in the discussion.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts intense AI discussion in technology circles with lower or varied awareness outside them, but it does not say that much of the wider public has yet to encounter AI.
